title: Eating Only Between 8 AM and 2 PM for Two Weeks Reduced Heart Inflammation in Heart Attack Survivors
excerpt: A randomised crossover trial published in the Journal of the American Heart Association found that a strict six-hour eating window lowered neutrophil counts, shifted monocyte gene expression toward anti-inflammatory patterns, and cut low-grade systemic inflammation in patients with established coronary artery disease.
body:
For decades, dietary advice for heart patients has focused on what to eat — less sodium, more fibre, fewer saturated fats. A new study asks a different question: **when** you eat may matter just as much, and possibly more, when it comes to the chronic inflammation that drives heart disease forward after a heart attack.

Published in the *Journal of the American Heart Association* in June 2026, the randomised crossover trial enrolled 19 patients with a prior myocardial infarction — a heart attack — and assigned them to either a two-week time-restricted eating (TRE) intervention or a two-week control period on their normal diet. After a washout of at least six weeks, each participant crossed over to the opposite group.

The TRE protocol was strict: participants could eat only between 8 AM and 2 PM, a six-hour window that ended well before the evening meal most people are accustomed to. Blood samples were drawn in a fasted state before and after each period.

## What Changed in Two Weeks

The results were striking for such a short intervention. Compared with the control diet, the TRE period produced:

- **Lower neutrophil counts** — neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells and key drivers of the inflammatory cascade that destabilises arterial plaques after a heart attack.
- **A reduced neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR)** — a well-established clinical marker of systemic inflammation and cardiovascular risk that is inexpensive to measure from a standard blood draw.
- **Decreased neutrophil CD11b expression** — CD11b is a surface marker involved in immune cell adhesion and tissue infiltration; its reduction suggests less aggressive immune cell behaviour at the vessel wall.
- **Anti-inflammatory changes in the monocyte transcriptome** — gene expression in monocytes shifted away from pro-inflammatory pathways. Monocytes are the cells that infiltrate artery walls and become the foam cells at the heart of atherosclerotic plaques.
- **Widespread metabolic changes** — metabolomic profiling revealed broad shifts in circulating metabolites, though the study did not detail individual compounds.
- **A reduction in low-grade systemic inflammation** — the chronic, simmering inflammation that underlies atherosclerosis progression.

Notably, there were no significant changes in monocyte subsets (the proportions of classical, intermediate, and non-classical monocytes), monocyte surface marker expression, or cytokine production capacity. The TRE effect appears to operate through the innate immune cell count and gene expression level rather than by reprogramming cytokine output.



> **"- **Anti-inflammatory changes in the monocyte transcriptome** — gene expression in monocytes shifted away from pro-inflammatory pathways."**


## Why This Matters for Heart Patients

The conventional view of time-restricted eating has focused on its metabolic benefits — weight loss, improved insulin sensitivity, better blood sugar control. A major network meta-analysis published in the BMJ in early 2026 confirmed that TRE, especially when the eating window is shifted early in the day, improves body weight, BMI, fat mass, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, and triglycerides compared with a normal diet.

But the new JAHA study goes further. It suggests that TRE directly modulates the immune cells that drive cardiovascular disease progression — not just the metabolic risk factors. This is an important distinction. A heart attack survivor can have perfect cholesterol and still suffer a second event if the inflammatory milieu in their arteries remains hostile.

> "Our findings highlight the capability of TRE in the modulation of inflammation, suggesting a potential role in reducing cardiovascular risk in patients with established cardiovascular disease."

The six-hour morning eating window used in this study is more restrictive than the 16:8 protocol popular among intermittent fasting enthusiasts. And the shift toward morning eating aligns with accumulating evidence that early TRE — finishing food intake by early afternoon — delivers superior metabolic outcomes compared with late-evening eating windows.

## The South Asian Heart Risk Factor

This research has particular relevance for the South Asian diaspora. Indians, Pakistanis, Bangladeshis, and Sri Lankans face a cardiovascular disease burden that is disproportionate to their metabolic profiles. The INTERHEART study famously showed that South Asians suffer heart attacks a decade earlier than other populations, driven by a combination of genetic predisposition, visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and elevated inflammatory markers.

For NRIs and their families, the appeal of time-restricted eating is its simplicity. It requires no special foods, no supplements, no prescriptions. It can be layered onto any cuisine, including traditional Indian vegetarian or non-vegetarian diets. And unlike pharmaceutical interventions, it carries minimal cost.

The practical challenge, of course, is cultural. Evening meals are central to South Asian family life — dinner is often the largest meal, served at 8 or 9 PM, followed by dessert and tea. An 8 AM to 2 PM eating window would require a fundamental restructuring of daily routines, one that may be easier for retirees and remote workers than for families with school-age children or evening social obligations.

## Caveats and Context

The study has important limitations. The sample size — 19 patients — is small, and 89 percent of participants were male, limiting generalisability. The two-week intervention is too short to assess sustained compliance, weight changes, or hard cardiovascular outcomes like recurrent heart attacks or death. And the crossover design, while rigorous, means each participant served as their own control — individual variation in diet quality, exercise, sleep, and medication adherence during the control period could confound results.

There is also the shadow of the controversial AHA abstract from 2024, which linked 8-hour time-restricted eating to a 91 percent higher risk of cardiovascular death in a large observational study. That finding was widely criticised for its methodology — the eating window was estimated from two days of dietary recall and extrapolated to years of follow-up — but it injected caution into the field.

This new trial, by contrast, directly measured immune cell behaviour under controlled conditions. The two studies are not contradictory so much as they are asking different questions: one about long-term mortality associations, the other about short-term biological mechanisms.

For heart patients interested in TRE, the practical takeaway is to discuss it with a cardiologist, start with a wider window like 10 hours, and shift meals earlier in the day. The evidence that morning eating is metabolically superior to evening eating is now consistent across multiple studies and populations.
